title: Snakebite Envenomation: Anti-Snake Venom, Neurotoxic and Haemotoxic Pathways (India)

evidenceAudit.scope: Snakebite in adults and children in India: first aid, antivenom indications and dosing, neurotoxic and haemotoxic care, referral.
findings: Every dose and threshold checked against the MoHFW STG 2017 page cited.
unverifiedSections: The guideline's antibiotic recommendations conflict between pages (prophylaxis versus no prophylaxis), so routine antibiotics are not included.
Normal laboratory ranges are typical adult ranges; laboratories differ.

pathophysiology.summary: Snakebite is a medical emergency across rural India, where the main medically important species are the spectacled cobra, the common krait, Russell's viper and the saw-scaled viper. Venoms are mixtures of enzymes and toxins whose effects fall into two broad syndromes that drive treatment. Elapid venoms from cobras and kraits are neurotoxic: cobra toxins block acetylcholine receptors at the neuromuscular junction, so the paralysis can partly reverse with anticholinesterase therapy, while krait toxins damage the nerve terminal before the junction, so paralysis is slow to recover and does not respond to neostigmine. Paralysis typically starts with ptosis and external ophthalmoplegia, then spreads to bulbar, neck-flexor and respiratory muscles; death follows from respiratory failure unless the airway is protected and ventilation supported. Viper venoms are haemotoxic: procoagulant enzymes consume fibrinogen and clotting factors, producing venom-induced consumption coagulopathy with incoagulable blood, spontaneous bleeding and bleeding from venepuncture sites, while other components injure the vascular endothelium, kidneys and muscle. Acute kidney injury from Russell's viper envenoming is a major cause of death and disability. Local tissue injury causes swelling, blistering and necrosis, and rising compartment pressure can threaten the limb. The 20-minute whole blood clotting test detects the coagulopathy at the bedside. Polyvalent anti-snake venom is raised in horses against the four main species; it neutralises circulating venom but cannot reverse established tissue damage, so it must be given early, intravenously and in full doses whenever signs of systemic envenomation appear. Because antivenom is a foreign protein, early anaphylactic reactions and late serum-sickness reactions occur and must be anticipated (MoHFW Standard Treatment Guidelines 2017).
keyMechanisms: Cobra neurotoxins block postsynaptic acetylcholine receptors, causing ptosis, bulbar and respiratory paralysis that may respond to atropine–neostigmine (STG 2017, pp. 35–36).
Krait toxins act before the junction, so paralysis recovers slowly and does not respond to neostigmine (STG 2017, p. 35).
Viper procoagulant enzymes consume clotting factors, producing incoagulable blood detected by the 20-minute whole blood clotting test (STG 2017, p. 21).
Haemotoxic envenoming injures the kidney, causing acute kidney injury that may need dialysis (STG 2017, pp. 37–39).
Local venom effects cause swelling, blistering, necrosis and compartment syndrome (STG 2017, pp. 45–46).

clinicalManagement.title: First aid and triage
actions: Reassure, immobilise the limb with a splint, keep nil by mouth and remove rings, watches and tight clothing (STG 2017, p. 8).
Do not cut, suck or wash the wound; do not apply tourniquets; do not give antivenom locally or intramuscularly (STG 2017, p. 9).
Assess airway, breathing and circulation first; secure IV access with normal saline (STG 2017, pp. 10, 18).
Draw blood for grouping and the 20-minute whole blood clotting test before antivenom (STG 2017, pp. 21–22).
Admit every suspected bite and observe for 24 hours (STG 2017, p. 10).
Check the distal pulse; release only after the antivenom loading dose has started (STG 2017, p. 19).
Give oxygen and assist ventilation (bag-valve, laryngeal mask or intubation) while antivenom is started (STG 2017, p. 35).

clinicalManagement.title: Give anti-snake venom for systemic envenomation
clinicalManagement.timeframe: As soon as any systemic sign appears — do not wait for laboratory results
actions: Give antivenom IV only, as an infusion over 30 minutes with a physician present; never as a test dose (STG 2017, pp. 28–31).
Observe every 5 minutes for 30 minutes, then every 15 minutes for 2 hours (STG 2017, p. 29).
Children receive the same number of vials as adults, diluted in 5–10 mL/kg normal saline with the bottle limited to 200 mL (STG 2017, p. 30).
10 vials over 30 minutes; a second 10 vials if there is no improvement within the first hour; maximum 20 vials (STG 2017, pp. 28, 31).
Loading dose 10 vials (Russell's viper) or 6 vials (saw-scaled viper) over 30 minutes (STG 2017, p. 28).
Repeat the clotting test 6-hourly and give antivenom 6-hourly until coagulation is restored; reconsider after 30 vials (STG 2017, p. 30).
Stop antivenom, give oxygen and adrenaline 0.5 mg IM (children 0.01 mg/kg), then restart slowly over 10–15 minutes once recovered (STG 2017, pp. 32–33).

clinicalManagement.title: Neurotoxic and haemotoxic supportive care
actions: Keep urine output at 1 mL/kg/h; monitor vital signs, bleeding, ptosis and paralysis every 1–2 hours (STG 2017, pp. 19, 37).
Do not give sedatives, morphine, pethidine or neuromuscular blockers in neurotoxic envenoming (STG 2017 Quick Reference, p. 39).
Avoid heparin and antifibrinolytics; give fresh frozen plasma 10–15 mL/kg for persistent coagulopathy with bleeding (STG 2017 Quick Reference, p. 37).
Give the atropine–neostigmine trial; stop after 3 doses without at least 50% recovery of ptosis (STG 2017, p. 36).
Do not give atropine–neostigmine (STG 2017, p. 35).
Urea above 130 mg/dL, creatinine above 4 mg/dL, potassium above 7 mmol/L or pulmonary oedema: arrange haemodialysis (STG 2017, p. 39).

clinicalManagement.title: Referral, wound care and surgery
actions: Refer if antivenom is unavailable (confirm stock by phone), for kidney injury, persistent coagulopathy or ventilator need (STG 2017, pp. 51–53).
Clean the wound with povidone-iodine, leave blisters intact and elevate the limb for spreading oedema (STG 2017, pp. 45–46).
Consider fasciotomy only for clinical compartment syndrome with pressure above 40 mmHg after coagulopathy is corrected (STG 2017, p. 46).
Give a tetanus toxoid booster after coagulopathy is corrected (STG 2017, p. 45).

title: Animal Bites and Rabies Post-Exposure Prophylaxis (India)
specialty: Emergency Medicine / Infectious Diseases / Primary Care

evidenceAudit.scope: Rabies post-exposure prophylaxis after animal bites in India.
findings: Regimens checked against the NCDC expert group minutes (2019) and the CDSCO SmPC.
unverifiedSections: The full National Guidelines on Rabies Prophylaxis document was not opened; the 2019 expert-group minutes record the retained regimens.

pathophysiology.summary: Rabies is an almost universally fatal viral encephalomyelitis, and India carries a large share of the global burden, mainly from dog bites. The rabies virus, a lyssavirus, is present in the saliva of an infected animal and enters the body through a bite, a scratch that draws blood, or contact of saliva with broken skin or mucous membranes. After entry the virus may replicate briefly in muscle at the wound, then binds to nerve endings and travels slowly along peripheral nerves to the spinal cord and brain. This incubation period usually lasts weeks to months, which is the window in which post-exposure prophylaxis works. Prophylaxis has three parts. Immediate and thorough washing of the wound with soap and running water for up to 15 minutes physically removes virus. Rabies immunoglobulin, infiltrated into and around every wound, neutralises virus at the site before the vaccine-induced antibody response develops. A full course of cell-culture rabies vaccine then produces neutralising antibodies that prevent the virus reaching the nervous system. Once the virus is in the central nervous system and symptoms appear, there is no effective treatment: patients develop either furious rabies with hydrophobia, aerophobia and agitation, or paralytic rabies, and death follows. Prophylaxis must therefore never be delayed while waiting to observe the animal or for laboratory confirmation. Previously vaccinated people need only short booster courses without immunoglobulin. India's national guidance retains rabies immunoglobulin for every category III exposure and supports the intradermal Updated Thai Red Cross regimen to save vaccine (NCDC expert group, January 2019).
keyMechanisms: Virus in animal saliva enters through bites, scratches that draw blood, or mucosal contact.
The virus travels slowly along peripheral nerves to the spinal cord and brain, giving an incubation period of weeks to months.
Wound washing, immunoglobulin at the wound and vaccination neutralise the virus before it reaches the nervous system (NCDC 2019).
Once encephalitis develops there is no effective treatment, so prophylaxis is time-critical.

pathophysiology.summary: Scorpion sting is common in rural India, particularly in Maharashtra, Karnataka, Andhra Pradesh, Telangana, Tamil Nadu and Gujarat, and the Indian red scorpion, Mesobuthus tamulus, causes most severe envenoming. Its venom contains toxins that keep sodium channels on nerve membranes open, producing a massive release of neurotransmitters from both arms of the autonomic nervous system. The resulting autonomic storm explains the clinical course. Early cholinergic effects include vomiting, profuse sweating, salivation, priapism and bradycardia. These are followed by an adrenergic phase with cold extremities, tachycardia and severe hypertension. Catecholamine excess causes myocardial injury and dysfunction, leading to acute heart failure, pulmonary oedema and cardiogenic shock, which are the usual causes of death, and children are at highest risk because of their small body size relative to the venom dose. Prazosin, an alpha-1 adrenergic blocker, counters the adrenergic effects, reverses peripheral vasoconstriction and reduces the load on the heart; it became the mainstay of treatment in India after it markedly reduced mortality. Scorpion antivenom neutralises circulating venom; Indian trials have studied monovalent antivenom given with prazosin, and the combination produced faster recovery than prazosin alone. Severity is judged clinically by grading local pain alone, autonomic features, and cardiovascular or respiratory compromise. Local pain is often intense and is treated with local anaesthetic infiltration and simple analgesia. Patients need close observation for several hours because cardiovascular complications can develop after an initially mild presentation.

pathophysiology.summary: Organophosphate and carbamate insecticides are among the most common causes of fatal poisoning in rural India, usually after deliberate ingestion, and sometimes after occupational skin or inhalational exposure. Both classes inhibit acetylcholinesterase, the enzyme that breaks down acetylcholine at nerve endings. Acetylcholine therefore accumulates at muscarinic receptors, nicotinic receptors and in the central nervous system, producing the cholinergic toxidrome. Muscarinic overstimulation causes bronchorrhoea, bronchospasm, salivation, lacrimation, urination, diarrhoea, vomiting, small pupils and bradycardia. The respiratory secretions and bronchospasm are the main early threat to life. Nicotinic overstimulation causes muscle fasciculations, weakness and paralysis, including of the respiratory muscles, and can produce tachycardia and hypertension. Central effects include agitation, confusion, seizures and coma. Organophosphates bind the enzyme in a way that becomes permanent over time, a process called ageing, whereas carbamate binding is reversible and effects are usually shorter. Atropine blocks muscarinic receptors and is the life-saving treatment; it is given in rapidly doubling doses until the chest is clear and the heart rate and blood pressure are adequate, then continued as an infusion. Oximes such as pralidoxime aim to reactivate the enzyme before ageing, but evidence of benefit is inconsistent. Between one and four days after ingestion some patients develop the intermediate syndrome, with weakness of neck-flexor, proximal limb and respiratory muscles that may require ventilation for days to weeks, so patients need close observation even after the cholinergic crisis has settled. Many pesticides are dissolved in hydrocarbon solvents, so aspiration pneumonitis is an added risk.

Nicotinic excess: fasciculations, weakness and respiratory muscle paralysis.
Intermediate syndrome 24–96 hours after ingestion causes neck-flexor, proximal and respiratory weakness (JNMA 2008, p. 254).
Atropine antagonises muscarinic effects; oximes may reactivate the enzyme before ageing.

pathophysiology.summary: Aluminium phosphide is a cheap grain fumigant sold in India as tablets, often under the name celphos, and is one of the most lethal poisons seen in Indian emergency departments; reported mortality within 24 hours ranges from 40% to over 90%. When the tablet meets water or stomach acid it releases phosphine gas, which is rapidly absorbed. Phosphine is a cellular poison: it inhibits mitochondrial respiration, particularly cytochrome c oxidase, and generates reactive oxygen species, so cells cannot produce energy and suffer oxidative damage. The heart is most affected. Myocardial depression and arrhythmias produce profound, often refractory cardiogenic shock, which is the main cause of death, and severe metabolic acidosis follows from tissue hypoperfusion and failed cellular metabolism. Other features include vomiting, epigastric pain, a garlic or fish-like odour, pulmonary oedema, acute kidney injury, liver injury and disturbances of potassium, magnesium and glucose. There is no specific antidote. Management is supportive and time-critical: early recognition, protection of the airway, careful fluid resuscitation guided by the circulation, correction of severe acidosis and electrolyte disturbances, and treatment of arrhythmias. Some centres have used extracorporeal membrane oxygenation to support the heart through the first days in refractory cardiogenic shock. Many traditional decontamination practices, such as potassium permanganate or bicarbonate lavage, lack scientific support, and an evidence review recommends oily agents rather than water-based solutions, because water accelerates phosphine release. Gastric lavage is not routinely recommended. Restricting access to the tablets is the most effective prevention.

pathophysiology.summary: Methanol poisoning in India usually occurs in outbreaks after consumption of illicit or adulterated liquor, and sometimes after ingestion of methanol-containing industrial products. Methanol itself is only mildly intoxicating; its toxicity comes from its metabolism. In the liver, alcohol dehydrogenase converts methanol to formaldehyde, which is rapidly oxidised to formic acid. Formic acid accumulates because humans clear it slowly, and it inhibits mitochondrial cytochrome oxidase, causing cellular hypoxia, lactic acidosis and a high anion gap metabolic acidosis. The optic nerve and retina, and the basal ganglia, are particularly vulnerable, producing blurred vision, reduced visual acuity and permanent blindness, and in severe cases brain injury and coma. Because metabolism takes time, symptoms typically begin 12 to 24 hours after drinking, and co-ingested ethanol can delay them further. Early on, the unmetabolised methanol raises the serum osmolality and creates an osmolar gap; later, as it is converted to formic acid, the osmolar gap falls while the anion gap rises. Treatment aims to block alcohol dehydrogenase so that no further formic acid is produced, to remove methanol and formate, and to correct acidosis. Fomepizole and ethanol both inhibit alcohol dehydrogenase; fomepizole is preferred where available, but ethanol is widely used in India because fomepizole is often unavailable. Folinic acid or folic acid speeds the breakdown of formate. Sodium bicarbonate corrects acidosis, and haemodialysis removes both methanol and formate and is decided with a toxicologist. Because outbreaks affect many people at once, early case finding among others who drank the same liquor saves lives.

clinicalManagement.title: Recognise and search for other cases
actions: Suspect methanol in anyone with acidosis or visual symptoms after illicit liquor, and alert public health to find others who drank the same batch.
Send blood gas, electrolytes, osmolality, glucose, ethanol and methanol levels where available.
Activated charcoal does not adsorb alcohols well (ISCCM 2024, Annexure 10).

clinicalManagement.title: Block alcohol dehydrogenase
clinicalManagement.timeframe: As soon as poisoning is suspected
actions: Fomepizole 15 mg/kg IV over 30 minutes, then 10 mg/kg every 12 hours for 4 doses, then 15 mg/kg every 12 hours (Austin guideline).
If fomepizole is unavailable: ethanol 10% IV 8–10 mL/kg over 30 minutes, then 1–2 mL/kg/h, targeting serum ethanol 22 mmol/L (Canadian Antidote Guide).
Fomepizole may be delayed until serum ethanol falls below 23 mmol/L (toxic alcohol resource, p. 2).

clinicalManagement.title: Folinic acid, bicarbonate and dialysis
actions: Folinic acid 1–2 mg/kg IV (maximum 50 mg) every 4–6 hours until methanol is below 6.25 mmol/L and acidosis has resolved (toxic alcohol resource, p. 3).
Sodium bicarbonate to keep pH above 7.2 (toxic alcohol resource, p. 3).
Decide on haemodialysis with a toxicologist; during dialysis give fomepizole every 4 hours or increase the ethanol infusion (Austin guideline; Canadian Antidote Guide).

clinicalManagement.title: Stop treatment at defined end-points
actions: Stop antidotes when methanol is below 6.25 mmol/L and acidosis is corrected, or the osmol gap is below 10 with pH above 7.3.
